title: Teachers Love Theories
author: Michael Pershan
summary: Michael Pershan argues that the education books that become massive bestsellers, Building Thinking Classrooms, Mathematical Mindsets, Carol Dweck's Mindset, all share a specific formula: a big explanatory theory paired with a handful of simple, adoptable techniques. Using Mindset as his case study, he shows how the theory of growth versus fixed mindsets only became culturally huge once it generated concrete actions like 'praise effort, not intelligence,' arguing the practical stuff would feel inert without the theory to make it feel meaningful, and the theory would feel abstract without the practices to make it actionable. He applies the same analysis to Peter Liljedahl's Building Thinking Classrooms, noting that despite dozens of interlocking practices the book demands as a package, only two, vertical whiteboards and random grouping, have actually spread widely among teachers, who treat doing those two things as equivalent to 'doing BTC' even while ignoring the rest. Drawing on David Tyack and Larry Cuban's concept of 'instructional add-ons,' Pershan predicts the big theory eventually fades from memory while the surviving practices get absorbed piecemeal into ordinary teaching, and argues this isn't really an indictment of teachers so much as evidence that teaching is confusing, high-volume work and people reasonably want theories to make sense of the chaos, even at the cost of full fidelity.
points: Pershan argues bestselling education books need both a big explanatory theory and a few simple techniques, using Mindset's 'praise effort, not intelligence' as the paradigm case of a technique made meaningful by its theory.

He shows that Building Thinking Classrooms's actual adoption reduces almost entirely to two practices, vertical non-permanent surfaces and random grouping, even though the book insists on wholesale implementation.
He invokes Tyack and Cuban's concept of 'instructional add-ons' to predict that the theory behind any bestseller eventually fades while a few surviving practices get absorbed into ordinary teaching.

His closing argument reframes selective, partial adoption not as teacher laziness but as a rational response to the constraints (time, administration, competing priorities) that make full-fidelity implementation unrealistic.
quotes: What makes these books so popular? One thing they do, I think it might be a characteristic of all world-beating ideas, is combine a big, explanatory theory with a few handy techniques that anybody can try.
Without theory this practical stuff would feel inert. Combine theory with practice, though, and it's magic.
There are tons of teachers whose use of BTC extends to almost nothing beyond these two practices. It's the "praising effort" of Liljedahl's approach.
The irony is that you need to go big and comprehensive if you want your small practical ideas to spread.
The big radical ideas get digested by the teaching profession until all that’s left are those catnip practices.
We need theories to help make sense of this mess. We want labels and categories and explanations to help us make order out of the chaos.
Look around at what resonates with people, there is a desperate, aching need for ideas, the bigger the better, and that's not going to change any time soon at all.
